newsitem.title: USA: Maine salmon farmers in trade dispute with Chile.
newsitem.headline: Maine salmon farmers in trade dispute with Chile.

text.p: A trade dispute is brewing between salmon farmers in Maine and Chile over the multimillion-dollar traffic in Atlantic salmon, an increasingly common commodity in U.S. supermarkets and restaurants.

A Maine-based industry group, Coalition for Fair Atlantic Salmon Trade, said it was considering filing an anti-dumping complaint alleging that Chilean salmon was being sold in the United States at below production cost.

The filing of such a complaint with the U.S. Commerce Department could lead to the swift imposition of tariffs against U.S. importers, a move that could dent a Chilean industry that exported $490 million in salmon last year, and damage burgeoning import businesses in Miami.

"This is a real threat," said Felipe Cubillos, senior advisor for the Association of Chilean Salmon and Trout Farmers, who denied Chile was dumping salmon. "This action will not solve their problems. It will create new problems."

Chile, which created its salmon farming industry only a decade ago to exploit natural advantages in climate and water, has become the second largest producer of farmed salmon in the world, behind only Norway. Last year it produced 100,000 metric tons and this year expects that figure to rise to 140,000 tons, according to the Association.
The United States is Chile's second-largest market behind Japan, buying 30 percent of its production, Cubillos said.

By contrast, the Maine industry produces just over 10 metric tons per year, a small fraction of the U.S. market, said Joseph McGonigle, managing director of the Coalition for Fair Atlantic Salmon Trade.

"Our share of the U.S. market is under 5 percent. Given an opportunity to gear up, we could serve the majority of the American market," said McGonigle. "In theory, if we had a closed market here, we could serve the whole thing."

But McGonigle said Maine farmers do not want a closed market, simply a "level playing field," and are considering seeking compensation in the form of a dumping action that could result in duties against importers that would bring the price of Chilean fish up to the cost of production.
"We believe that the likely low for production in Chile is somewhere in the $1.25-$1.30-a-pound range," he said. "We've seen fish coming in for ... in the area of 98 cents-$1.00."
Cubillos denied that Chile was dumping salmon in the U.S. market, but said it was difficult to determine production cost for the fish because it varied from farmer to farmer.
The Chilean industry has created 5,000 U.S. jobs -- compared to 500 workers in the Maine industry -- which would be at risk if duties were imposed, he said.
"This is not a problem between American workers and foreign workers," said Cubillos. "We give more jobs in the U.S. than the Maine industry."

Trade experts said the dispute could chill the heated trade in Chilean salmon for a time but was unlikely to have any long-term impact on Chile's push to join the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).

"It cools off the trade. They (importers) don't want to risk being subjected to an uncertain duty," said Stephen Lande, a senior researcher with the University of Miami's North-South Centre and an expert on international trade.
Many of the U.S. jobs dependent on the Chilean industry -- which estimates its U.S. economic impact at $350 million annually -- are with Miami importers and freight forwarders.

"Any reduction in the volume of salmon coming into the country will have a direct impact," said Daniel Schneider of Rank International Forwarding in Miami. "Sixty percent of our business is the receiving and handling of Chilean salmon."
David Solomon, chief executive of Aquafarms International, a Miami importer, said a tariff on Chilean salmon could drive smaller companies out of business.
"There would be uncertainty in the market," said Solomon. "If there are duties imposed, a lot of the marginal businesses involved in Chilean salmon will be gone."
Cubillos said the best solution for Maine farmers would be to invest in Chile. "If they cannot grow cost-effectively in their area, why not invest in the area that can do it?"
